title: Browser text rules
summary: This module is the JavaScript port of `rag/normalize.py`, the line-unwrap rule of `rag/ingest.py` and the chunker of `rag/chunking.py`. The browser demo needs it twice: to tokenise your question for BM25 exactly the way Python tokenised the sample documents, and to chunk files you upload in the browser with the same rules. Text goes in; normalised text, BM25 tokens, a language code, sentences or chunks come out, identical to what the Python functions return.

key_ideas.explain: If the browser tokenised «الإجازة» differently from Python, BM25 would compare different token forms and miss matches. That is why every regex and step here mirrors `rag/normalize.py`, and why the stopword lists and prefixes are loaded from `index.json` instead of being copied by hand.
`export function ...` makes a function importable by other files with `import { tokenize } from "./text.js"`. Each `.js` file is its own module with its own scope, like a Python module.

A JS regex literal is `/pattern/flags`. `g` (global) makes `match` return every match and `replace` replace every match, which Python's `findall` and `sub` do by default. `u` turns on Unicode mode, needed for property classes like `\p{L}` (any letter in any script).
`(?<=...)` and `(?<!...)` check what comes before a position without consuming it, exactly as in Python. All current browsers support them, so the sentence and line-wrap rules port unchanged.

blocks.note: Header comment: this file is a rule-for-rule port of three Python modules, so uploaded files get the same cleaning, sentence splitting, chunking and BM25 tokenisation as the documents indexed in Python. Line 4 is blank.
Section comment: the normalisation part, mirroring `rag/normalize.py`.

L6: `TASHKEEL`, the same diacritic code-point ranges as `_TASHKEEL` in `rag/normalize.py`, written as literal characters. The `g` flag makes `replace` remove every occurrence; without it JavaScript replaces only the first match.
L7: `TATWEEL`, the kashida ـ, also global.
L8: `INVISIBLE`, zero-width and bidi control characters, the same ranges as Python's `_INVISIBLE`.

`ARABIC_DIGITS` matches Arabic-Indic digits ٠ to ٩ and Extended Arabic-Indic digits ۰ to ۹. Python uses a `str.maketrans` table; JavaScript has no translate method, so a regex plus a replacement function (`digitToAscii` below) does the same job.

`TOKEN` is identical to Python's `_TOKEN`: a number with optional decimal part, a run of lowercase Latin letters, or a run of Arabic letters ء to ي. With the `g` flag, `str.match(TOKEN)` returns all matches, like `re.findall`.

`ARABIC_CHAR` tests whether a character is in the Arabic block U+0600 to U+06FF. No `g` flag here on purpose: a global regex used with `.test()` remembers its position between calls (`lastIndex`), which causes confusing alternating results. Line 12 is blank.

`let` declares module-level variables that can be reassigned later (`const` could not be). They start empty and are filled by `configure` once `index.json` is loaded. `new Set()` is JavaScript's set type, with `has`, `add` and `size`. Line 15 is blank.

L16 to L17: the comment gives the reason: the lists come from `index.json`, written by `scripts/export_web_index.py`, so Python and the browser always share them.
L18: `configure({ stopwords_en, stopwords_ar, ar_prefixes })` uses **object destructuring** in the parameter list: the function receives the whole config object and pulls out just these three properties by name.
L19: builds one `Set` of both stopword lists. `[...a, ...b]` is the **spread** syntax: it expands both arrays into a new array, like `[*a, *b]` in Python.
L20: keeps the prefix list in Python's order (longest first), which matters because the first matching prefix wins.
L21: end of function.

L22: blank.
L23: `digitToAscii` is the replacement function for `ARABIC_DIGITS`: `replace` calls it with each matched digit.
L24: `charCodeAt(0)` returns the UTF-16 code of the character, for example 0x0663 for ٣.
L25: Extended digits start at 0x06F0 and Arabic-Indic digits at 0x0660, so subtracting the right base gives the digit value 0 to 9, which `String(...)` turns into `"3"`.
L26 to L27: end of function, blank.
`normalizeForMatch` is the port of Python's `normalize_for_match`, written as a **method chain**: each `.replace` returns a new string that the next call works on.

L30: `.normalize("NFKC")`, the same Unicode normalisation as `unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", ...)`: ligatures like ﻻ become لا.
L31: removes invisible marks.
L32 to L33: removes tashkeel and tatweel, Python's `strip_tashkeel`.

L34: alef forms آ أ إ ٱ become bare ا.
L35: alef maqsura ى becomes ي.
L36: taa marbuta ة becomes ه, so «إجازة» ends up as `اجازه`, the same as in Python.
L37: hamza on waw or yaa (ؤ ئ) becomes ء.

L38: maps Eastern digits to ASCII by passing a function as the replacement: «٣٠٠» becomes `300`.
L39: lowercases Latin text.
L40: end of function.

L41: blank.
L42: `tokenize(text, removeStopwords = true)` has a **default parameter value**, like Python's `remove_stopwords=True`. JavaScript has no keyword-only arguments, so callers pass `false` positionally.
L43: the output array.

Loops over every token of the normalised text. `match` returns `null` when nothing matches, so `|| []` falls back to an empty array (Python's `findall` would already return `[]`). `let tok` because the loop body may replace the token.
Skips stopwords with `Set.has`. Python checks two sets; here they were merged into one in `configure`. `continue` jumps to the next token, as in Python.

L46: if the token's first character is Arabic (Python's `_ARABIC_CHAR.match(tok)` also tests only the start).
L47: `Array.find` returns the first prefix that the token starts with and that leaves at least 3 letters, or `undefined`. `(pre) => ...` is an **arrow function**, JavaScript's short lambda.
L48: if one was found, cuts it off with `slice`. «الفلتر» becomes «فلتر».
Otherwise, the same naive plural fold as Python: a Latin token longer than 3 letters ending in `s` but not `ss` loses the final `s`, so "days" becomes "day". `slice(0, -1)` is `tok[:-1]`.
Appends the token, returns the list. Lines 55 and 56 close the function and add a blank line.

L57: `detectLanguage`, the port of `detect_language`.
L58: counts Arabic-block characters. `/[...]/g` with `match` returns all matches (or `null`, hence `|| []`), and `.length` counts them.
L59: counts ASCII letters.
L60: Arabic only if it strictly wins, using the ternary operator `cond ? a : b` (Python's `a if cond else b`).
L61 to L62: end of function, blank.

L63 to L64: `cleanText`, the port of `clean_text`: readable cleanup for stored and displayed text.
L65: NFKC.
L66 to L67: removes invisible marks and tatweel, but keeps tashkeel and letter forms, so quotes look exactly like the document.

L68: collapses spaces, tabs and no-break spaces (a literal U+00A0 in the class) into one space.
L69: removes spaces around newlines.
L70: three or more newlines become two.
L71: `.trim()` is Python's `.strip()`.
L72 to L73: end of function, blank.

L74: section comment for the ingest rule.
L75 to L76: the same explanation as in `rag/ingest.py`: a newline before a lowercase letter, digit or bracket, not after sentence punctuation, is a PDF line wrap.
L77 to L79: `unwrapLines` uses the same regex with a negative **lookbehind** `(?<![.!?:؟])` and a lookahead `(?=[a-z0-9(])`, replacing each wrap newline with a space.
L80: blank.

L81: section comment for chunking.
L82: `SENT_END` is Python's `_SENT_END`: whitespace after `.`, `!`, `?`, `؟` or `。` (a **lookbehind** `(?<=...)` keeps the punctuation with its sentence), or one or more newlines.
L83: `EDGE` strips spaces, `>`, `-`, `*` and tabs from both ends of a sentence. JavaScript's `trim()` cannot take a character list like Python's `strip(" >-*\t")`, so a regex anchored at the start (`^`) or end (`$`) does it.
L84: blank.

`splitSentences`, the port of `split_sentences`. `split(SENT_END)` cuts the text into pieces; `.map(...)` transforms each piece (remove a leading `#` heading marker, trim, strip the edge characters); `.filter(Boolean)` drops empty strings, because `Boolean("")` is false. This is the chained form of Python's generator expression plus list comprehension. Line 91 is blank.

`simpleTokenCount`, the port of `simple_token_count`: a run of word characters or a single other non-space character counts as one token. Python's `\w` is Unicode-aware by default; JavaScript's `\w` is ASCII only, so the port spells it out as `[\p{L}\p{N}_]` (any letter, any number, underscore), which needs the `u` flag. Uploads in the browser are actually counted with the e5 tokenizer (`Engine.countTokens`); this is the fallback default. Line 95 is blank.
`splitLong`, the port of `_split_long`, for one sentence longer than the token budget. `out` collects pieces, `cur` holds the words of the current piece (`let` because it is reassigned).

L99: splits on whitespace and drops empty strings (Python's `split()` with no argument does both at once). `for (const w of ...)` iterates values, like Python's `for w in ...`.
L100: if the current piece is non-empty and adding this word would exceed the budget, the piece is finished. `[...cur, w]` builds a new array without changing `cur`.
L101 to L102: saves the piece and starts a new one.
L104: adds the word. A single word longer than the budget still becomes its own piece.
L103, L105: closing braces.
Saves the last piece, returns the list, closes the function. Line 109 is blank.

L110 to L111: the comment restates the chunking rule from `rag/chunking.py`: pack sentences up to `maxTokens`, start the next chunk with the last sentences of the previous one up to `overlapTokens`, so a fact on a boundary is never lost.
L112: `chunkPages(pages, { maxTokens = 160, overlapTokens = 40, count = simpleTokenCount } = {})` is JavaScript's version of keyword arguments: an options object, destructured with defaults, and `= {}` so it can be omitted entirely.
L113: the output array.

L114: page by page, so a chunk never spans pages.
L115: `sents` holds `[sentence, tokenCount]` pairs (two-element arrays play the role of Python tuples).
L116 to L117: a sentence within budget stays whole, a longer one is split on words.
L118: stores each piece with its count, computed once.
L119: closes the loop.
`n` numbers chunks on the page, `i` is the first sentence of the next chunk; loop until all sentences are placed.

L123 to L125: a new chunk: its sentences, its token size, a cursor `j`.
L126: adds sentences while they fit; `!cur.length` always admits the first one, so the loop progresses.
L127 to L129: adds the sentence and its count, moves on.
L130: closes the inner loop.

L131: joins the sentences with newlines.
L132: pushes a plain object with the same fields as Python's `Chunk`. The id uses a **template literal** (backticks, `${...}` placeholders, like an f-string): `travel-policy.en.pdf#p2-c0`. `{ ..., text, ... }` is **shorthand** for `text: text`.
L133: next chunk number.
L134: last sentence used: the page is done.

The overlap step, line for line the same as Python: walk back over trailing sentences while they fit in `overlapTokens`, but never back to the chunk's first sentence (`k - 1 > i`), so the next chunk always starts later. `i = k` starts the next chunk on the overlap.
Closes the loops, returns all chunks and closes the function. Line 146 is blank.

L147 to L148: the comment points at the source: `is_answer_candidate` in `rag/generate.py`.
L149 to L150: trims the sentence.
L151: at least 4 tokens counting stopwords (`tokenize(s, false)`), and not ending in `?` or `؟`. `/[?؟]$/.test(s)` checks the last character with a regex anchored at the end.
L152: end of function.
